Traditions aren't fixed things: they change all the time, and courts and legislatures in many countries have already recognized that a cultural practice isn't immune from the ban on cruelty to animals.
"We've always eaten meat. My grandparents ate it, my parents ate it; it's not going to change now."
Practices that have survived for generations have passed a long test of social life.
What has passed that test deserves a presumption of legitimacy, and whoever wants to change it bears the burden of proof.
Eating animals is one of humanity's oldest and most widespread practices.
So eating animals is legitimate unless proven otherwise.
The strong version has a respectable inspiration: the idea, associated with Edmund Burke's conservatism, that old institutions hold an accumulated wisdom no individual can rebuild alone.

fails at P2: surviving for generations shows a practice was useful to those who kept it, not that it was just to those who paid for it. And even accepting the burden of proof, it has already been met in the chapters of family A.
"It's been this way for thousands of years."
"Humans have eaten meat since the caves."
"Do you think thousands of generations were wrong?"
"Established practices carry a wisdom that shouldn't be discarded without strong reasons."
"It's part of who we are." (which is D6 and D3)

Long ago, many things were considered normal that we now know were wrong. It was once normal to hit children to discipline them, and once normal that women couldn't vote. People had been doing these things for a long time, and they were still wrong. Doing something for a long time doesn't turn wrong into right. What matters is whether someone is being hurt.

How long something has been done doesn't tell you whether it's just. Slavery lasted for centuries and was abolished in the British Empire in 1833, in the United States in 1865 and in Brazil, the last country in the Americas, in 1888. Women won the vote in New Zealand in 1893, in Brazil in 1932 and, at the federal level, in Switzerland only in 1971. In each case, someone said "it's always been this way". Would you have accepted that argument back then? And traditions change all the time: the United Kingdom banned cockfighting and bull-baiting in 1835, and Brazil's Supreme Federal Court struck down the
, even though they were traditional practices, because they subjected animals to cruelty.
"Is there any old tradition you're glad came to an end?"
: treating the age of a practice as proof that it is right. The mistake is confusing two questions.
Yes, and that's a historical fact
Nothing. Age says nothing about justice

Tradition can explain why we do something. It can't justify it, because traditions were decided by those who benefited from them, without hearing from those who paid the price. Animals never took part in that "test of social life".

text.bold: 1. The phrase has defended almost every injustice.

paragraph.text: Slavery was a centuries-old tradition when it was abolished: in the British Empire, by a law of 1833; in the United States, by the Thirteenth Amendment, in 1865; in Brazil, the last country in the Americas to end it, in 1888; and in Mauritania, the last country in the world to abolish it officially, only in 1981, with criminal penalties only from 2007. Excluding women from the vote was a tradition too: New Zealand was the first country to grant women the vote in national elections, in 1893; Brazil did so in 1932; and Switzerland only in 1971, at the federal level. In each case, the change was presented as an attack on the natural order of things, and today almost no one regrets it.

Today's diet isn't our grandparents': cheap chicken and eating meat every day are recent phenomena, created by industrial animal farming. Whoever invokes tradition usually defends a habit that is a few decades old, not millennia.

text.bold: 3. The law has already answered the question.

paragraph.text: In 1835 the United Kingdom banned bull-baiting, bear-baiting and cockfighting, entertainments that had been traditional for centuries, and cockfighting is now illegal in every US state. In Brazil, the Supreme Federal Court ruled in 1997 that the
, a bull-chasing tradition in Santa Catarina, violates the constitutional ban on subjecting animals to cruelty. It did the same with cockfighting and, in 2016, with the
, a rodeo-like event, striking down a law of the state of Ceará. The reasoning was the same: a practice's cultural value doesn't make it immune from the other values protected by law.

text.bold: 4. The burden of proof has been met.

paragraph.text: The strong version accepts change when there are good reasons. The chapters of family A show that no criterion separates animals from protected humans without falling back on the arbitrariness of species. Tradition only works as a presumption until someone examines the question.

text.bold: 5. Tradition is also made by those who changed.

paragraph.text: Every moral tradition we value today began with someone who broke with the previous one. If no one could change what had always been done, the very tradition we're proud of wouldn't exist.

text.bold: 6. Even a people's reputation with animals changes.

paragraph.text: Today the British are known for their attachment to animals. But the political philosopher Alasdair Cochrane recalls that, before the nineteenth century, their European neighbors saw them as one of the peoples least affectionate toward animals, because of the popularity of bear- and badger-baiting and of dog- and cockfighting (Cochrane, 2010, p. 79). Cochrane also notes that the enormous meat consumption of today's rich societies is a new phenomenon, as the diets of recent ancestors show (Cochrane, 2010, pp. 137–138). What gets called "always" is usually a snapshot of a few generations.

"We've always done this" only becomes a reason to carry on through a premise that goes unsaid: "if we've always done something, it's permissible to keep doing it". The philosopher Nathan Nobis notes that, written out in full, this premise is very likely false (
, 2016, p. 52), and point 1 shows why: it would approve of every old injustice we now condemn.

(d) The strongest counter-reply: it isn't age, it's prudence

The most serious version doesn't say the old is right. It says that rapid, radical social change tends to have unforeseen consequences, and that tradition deserves caution: change slowly, test, keep what works. Asking a whole food culture to change is asking for an enormous transformation, and prudence advises distrusting anyone who promises everything will work out.

There's a truth in tradition. Practices that last generations carry real meaning: identity, memory, family gatherings. Hasty changes can also have costs we don't foresee, and it's sensible to respect the value people place on their roots, without treating them with contempt.

But what is valuable in tradition rarely depends on the victim. The gathering, the shared food and the memory of grandparents can continue without the animal on the plate. Respecting tradition doesn't require preserving what in it causes harm; it requires separating one from the other.
